package_info.package_manager: VMware ESXi hypervisor (not a package manager, but a platform)
package_info.package_versions: Domain-joined ESXi hypervisors prior to patched version (pre-June 2024 security update)
package_info.why_malicious: The vulnerability allows attackers to gain full administrative permissions on domain-joined ESXi hypervisors by manipulating or creating a group named 'ESX Admins' in Active Directory. This bypasses proper access control checks, enabling attackers to deploy ransomware, encrypt virtual machines, exfiltrate data, and move laterally within the environment.

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, when Active Directory group membership is evaluated by ESXi for access control
execution_context.file_location: Active Directory domain controller and ESXi access control logic (e.g., /etc/likewise/lsassd.conf or equivalent configuration files)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Create a new domain group named 'ESX Admins' or rename an existing group to 'ESX Admins' in Active Directory, then add attacker-controlled accounts to this group.
malicious_snippets.code_language: Active Directory administrative action (directory manipulation, not traditional code)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the attacker creates or renames a group to 'ESX Admins' in Active Directory and adds attacker-controlled accounts as members; when ESXi synchronizes with Active Directory, it recognizes this group as an admin group, granting full administrative access to its members, enabling privilege escalation.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Manipulating group names to match hardcoded admin group identifiers is a classic privilege escalation technique, especially when followed by the addition of unauthorized accounts.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal behavior expects group membership and access control to be based on explicit, secure configuration and validation, not solely on group name matching without verification of group origin or intent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate administrators may create or rename groups for organizational purposes, but not with the intent to bypass access controls or escalate privileges for unauthorized users.
key_indicators: Creation or renaming of a group named 'ESX Admins' in Active Directory
Addition of new or unusual accounts to the 'ESX Admins' group
Absence of corresponding legitimate administrative change requests or tickets
ESXi logs showing new administrative sessions from accounts recently added to 'ESX Admins'

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, after attacker-controlled accounts gain ESXi administrative access via 'ESX Admins' group membership

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Deploy and execute ransomware (e.g., Akira, Black Basta) on the ESXi hypervisor to encrypt virtual machine files and system data, optionally exfiltrating sensitive information.
malicious_snippets.code_language: Ransomware binary (typically ELF format for ESXi/Linux platforms)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: After gaining administrative access via the compromised 'ESX Admins' group, the attacker uploads and executes ransomware on the ESXi host; the ransomware enumerates and encrypts virtual machine files (e.g., .vmdk, .vmx), modifies system files, and may exfiltrate data to attacker-controlled infrastructure, resulting in denial of service and potential data loss.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Execution of ransomware on a hypervisor is highly anomalous and destructive, as it targets critical infrastructure and disrupts all hosted virtual machines.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal administrative actions do not involve mass encryption of VM files, modification of system files, or exfiltration of sensitive data from the hypervisor.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: There is no legitimate use case for encrypting all VM files or deploying ransomware binaries on ESXi hosts.
key_indicators: Presence or execution of known ransomware binaries (e.g., Akira, Black Basta) on ESXi hosts
Mass encryption or renaming of VM files (e.g., .vmdk, .vmx) with unusual extensions
Creation of ransom note files in VM directories
Unusual outbound network connections from ESXi host to external IPs or domains
Modification of /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, or group files on ESXi

attack_chain.action: Attacker creates or renames a group to 'ESX Admins' in Active Directory and adds attacker-controlled accounts to this group, or leverages an existing group with that name.
attack_chain.leads_to: Gains full administrative access to domain-joined ESXi hypervisors for attacker-controlled accounts.

attack_chain.action: Attacker uses new administrative privileges to deploy and execute ransomware on the ESXi hypervisor, encrypting VM files and potentially exfiltrating data.
attack_chain.leads_to: Denial of service for all hosted virtual machines, data loss, and potential lateral movement or data exfiltration.

behavioral_signatures: Creation or renaming of a group named 'ESX Admins' in Active Directory
Addition of new or unusual accounts to the 'ESX Admins' group
Unusual or first-time administrative access to ESXi hypervisors from accounts recently added to 'ESX Admins'
Mass encryption or renaming of VM files on ESXi hosts
Execution of unrecognized binaries or scripts on ESXi hosts
file_indicators: Presence of ransomware binaries (e.g., Akira, Black Basta) in /tmp/, /var/tmp/, or other writable directories on ESXi hosts
Unusual changes to /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, or group files on ESXi
VM files (e.g., .vmdk, .vmx) with encrypted extensions or ransom note files (e.g., README.txt, HOW_TO_DECRYPT.txt) in VM directories
network_indicators: Outbound connections from ESXi hosts to known ransomware command-and-control (C2) or exfiltration domains/IPs
Unusual SMB, RDP, or SSH activity originating from ESXi hosts
LDAP or Kerberos traffic from attacker-controlled hosts to Active Directory for group enumeration or manipulation
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Continuously monitor Active Directory for creation, renaming, or membership changes of the 'ESX Admins' group, especially the addition of new or unrecognized accounts. Correlate these events with ESXi logs for new administrative sessions or privilege escalations. Monitor ESXi hosts for execution of unrecognized binaries, mass file modifications, or the presence of ransomware indicators (e.g., encrypted VM files, ransom notes). Use SIEM/XDR queries to identify suspicious group changes, new administrative logins, and anomalous network activity from ESXi systems. Implement alerting for any combination of these behaviors to enable rapid detection and response.
